latestRelease.title: Release v2.14.5
latestRelease.notes:
## Changelog

Refer to the [2.14 Upgrade Guide](https://docs.nats.io/release-notes/whats_new/whats_new_214) for backwards compatibility notes with 2.12.x. Please note that the 2.13.x version was skipped.

### Go Version

- 1.26.5

### Dependencies

- github.com/klauspost/compress v1.19.2 (#8459)
- golang.org/x/crypto v0.55.0 (#8459)

### Added

Leafnodes

- New `dial_timeout` option can be specified in the `leafnode` config block or for specific remotes in the configuration, allowing it to be increased above the default 1 second for high-latency links (#8427)

### Fixed

General

- Fixed a deadlock that could occur in the logger when a close error occurs (#8430)

JetStream

- Fix a bug that could result in potential data loss when handling idempotent stream creates when an offline node catches up from a metalayer snapshot, caused by an incorrect update to the create time in the stream assignment (#8449)

### Complete Changes
 
https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/compare/v2.14.4...v2.14.5

signals.title: Apply clustered expected-last-subject-sequence checks during replicated apply
signals.text: ### Proposed change Make `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` an authoritative replicated condition for clustered streams. Today clustered publishing validates the condition before proposing the message. The condition itself is not authoritative during replicated apply: expected-subject in-flight state is leader-local, is cleared during a leader transition, and the clustered apply path deliberately skips the general consistency checks. The proposed implementation would preserve the existing pre-proposal check for fast feedback, while marking conditionally admitted replicated entries so every supporting replica rechecks the expected subject sequence against its applied stream state immediately before storage. A mismatch would deterministically reject the committed entry and advance failed-sequence accounting without storing or delivering the message. Atomic batches would reproduce the existing staged-batch restrictions and preflight all marked conditions under the stream lock before storing any batch member, preserving all-or-nothing behavior. For rolling-upgrade safety, the suggested rollout is: - all supporting binaries always understand and honor the replicated marker, regardless of their local proposal-side flag - proposal-side emission is initially behind a default-off feature flag - every possible stream peer must first run a supporting binary, then the flag must be enabled on every server that can lead the stream - effective support and enablement are verified per server through the existing startup log and `Varz.feature_flags` surface (absent = unsupported, `false` = supported but disabled, `true` = enabled) - unmarked historical entries retain their current behavior This proposal is intentionally limited to `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence`. It does not propose changing message headers, the public error model, sources/mirrors, other consistency headers, or adding a new client capability API. Before implementation I would appreciate confirmation that: 1. the replicated-marker/default-off rollout and existing operational verification surface are acceptable 2. applied per-subject store state is the intended deterministic basis for this check across supported retention modes 3. an apply-time mismatch should consume clustered failed-sequence accounting in the same way as another rejected committed stream entry 4. a marked entry with a missing or invalid predicate should fail closed as a malformed replicated command ### Use case `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` is used as subject-level optimistic concurrency control. A caller reads subject state at sequence S and publishes an update conditional on S still being current. For clustered streams, correctness currently depends on the leader's pre-proposal state and surrounding leadership/readiness mechanisms. The captured-term proposal fence prevents an old-term proposal, but it does not make the conditional predicate part of the replicated state-machine command. Current main has refused every transition route measured, and this proposal does not claim a reproduced production data-loss incident. The objective is to make the existing optimistic-concurrency condition authoritative at the state-machine boundary, so a committed entry whose predicate is stale cannot become valid merely because it crossed a leader transition or was replayed under different in-memory admission state. A deterministic regression can commit a current-term stale conditional entry after a newer value, proving that apply rejects it without relying on leader timing. Removing only the apply-time check then makes the stale value survive, which directly discriminates the proposed mechanism. ### Contribution Yes. I intend to contribute the implementation, including: - backward-compatible replicated encoding - default-off rollout flag and operational verification - normal, fast-batch, and atomic-batch handling - file- and memory-store tests - transform, explicit-subject, compression, restart, replay, catch-up, and sequence-accounting tests - source/mirror and feature-off compatibility tests - a deterministic apply-boundary regression and discriminating mutations

signals.title: JetStream file stream Created timestamp changes after restart and configuration update
signals.text: ### Observed behavior For a standalone file-backed JetStream stream, the `Created` timestamp stored in `meta.inf` can change after this sequence: 1. Create a stream. 2. Restart the server using the same store directory. 3. Update the stream configuration. 4. Restart the server again. After the first restart, the JetStream API still returns the original `Created` timestamp. However, the subsequent configuration update rewrites `meta.inf` using the first restart time. After the second restart, the changed timestamp is exposed through the API. This was initially observed with a KV bucket because `CreateOrUpdateKeyValue` performs a stream configuration update, but the issue is not KV-specific. This is particularly important because recent stream recreation detection uses the creation timestamp as part of the stream identity: - https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/pull/8384 - https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/pull/8413 This issue differs from https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/pull/8449. That PR preserves the creation timestamp in clustered stream assignments during an idempotent create. This issue occurs during standalone file stream recovery. ### Expected behavior A stream's `Created` timestamp should remain unchanged throughout the lifetime of the stream, including server restarts and configuration updates. It should change only when the stream is deleted and a new stream is created. ### Server and client version The standalone reproducer uses: ```text nats-server v2.14.4 nats.go v1.51.0 Go 1.25.12 ``` The issue was also reproduced against the current `nats-server` `main` branch: ```text 99bbfb98035f4f0df06333a9a280c0517eaeff1c ``` ### Host environment ```text Microsoft Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200 windows/amd64 ``` The issue appears platform-independent because it results from the in-memory recovery and filestore metadata update path. ### Steps to reproduce Create the following two files. <details> <summary>go.mod</summary> ```go module nats-created-repro go 1.25.0 require ( github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2 v2.14.4 github.com/nats-io/nats.go v1.51.0 ) ``` </details> <details> <summary>main.go</summary> ```go package main import ( "context" "encoding/json" "fmt" "log" "os" "path/filepath" "time" server "github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2/server" "github.com/nats-io/nats.go" "github.com/nats-io/nats.go/jetstream" ) const ( bucket = "REPRO" stream = "KV_" + bucket ) type instance struct { srv *server.Server conn *nats.Conn js jetstream.JetStream } func main() { dir := must(os.MkdirTemp("", "nats-created-repro-")) defer os.RemoveAll(dir) ctx := context.Background() // Run 1: create the KV bucket. n := start(dir) must(n.js.CreateOrUpdateKeyValue(ctx, jetstream.KeyValueConfig{ Bucket: bucket, Storage: jetstream.FileStorage, })) initialAPI := apiCreated(ctx, n.js) initialMeta := metaCreated(dir) n.stop() // Run 2: recover the stream and update its configuration. time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond) n = start(dir) beforeUpdateAPI := apiCreated(ctx, n.js) beforeUpdateMeta := metaCreated(dir) must(n.js.CreateOrUpdateKeyValue(ctx, jetstream.KeyValueConfig{ Bucket: bucket, Storage: jetstream.FileStorage, })) afterUpdateAPI := apiCreated(ctx, n.js) afterUpdateMeta := metaCreated(dir) n.stop() // Run 3: recover the stream from the rewritten meta.inf. n = start(dir) afterRestartAPI := apiCreated(ctx, n.js) n.stop() printTime("run 1 API Created", initialAPI) printTime("run 1 meta.inf Created", initialMeta) printTime("run 2 API before update", beforeUpdateAPI) printTime("run 2 meta.inf before update", beforeUpdateMeta) printTime("run 2 API after update", afterUpdateAPI) printTime("run 2 meta.inf after update", afterUpdateMeta) printTime("run 3 API after second restart", afterRestartAPI) if !initialAPI.Equal(initialMeta) || !beforeUpdateAPI.Equal(initialAPI) || !beforeUpdateMeta.Equal(initialMeta) || !afterUpdateAPI.Equal(initialAPI) || afterUpdateMeta.Equal(initialMeta) || !afterRestartAPI.Equal(afterUpdateMeta) { log.Fatal("BUG NOT REPRODUCED: unexpected timestamps") } fmt.Println("BUG REPRODUCED: CreateOrUpdateKeyValue changed Created after a restart") } func start(dir string) *instance { srv := must(server.NewServer(&server.Options{ Host: "127.0.0.1", Port: server.RANDOM_PORT, JetStream: true, StoreDir: dir, NoLog: true, NoSigs: true, })) go srv.Start() if !srv.ReadyForConnections(10 * time.Second) { log.Fatal("NATS server did not become ready") } conn := must(nats.Connect(srv.ClientURL())) return &instance{srv: srv, conn: conn, js: must(jetstream.New(conn))} } func (n *instance) stop() { n.conn.Close() n.srv.Shutdown() n.srv.WaitForShutdown() } func apiCreated(ctx context.Context, js jetstream.JetStream) time.Time { info := must(must(js.Stream(ctx, stream)).Info(ctx)) return info.Created } func metaCreated(dir string) time.Time { data := must(os.ReadFile(filepath.Join( dir, "jetstream", "$G", "streams", stream, "meta.inf", ))) var meta struct{ Created time.Time } if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &meta); err != nil { panic(err) } return meta.Created } func printTime(label string, value time.Time) { fmt.Printf("%-36s %s\n", label+":", value.Format(time.RFC3339Nano)) } func must[T any](value T, err error) T { if err != nil { panic(err) } return value } ``` </details> Run: ```shell go mod tidy go run . ``` Example output: ```text run 1 API Created: 2026-08-15T20:22:22.3732008Z run 1 meta.inf Created: 2026-08-15T20:22:22.3732008Z run 2 API before update: 2026-08-15T20:22:22.3732008Z run 2 meta.inf before update: 2026-08-15T20:22:22.3732008Z run 2 API after update: 2026-08-15T20:22:22.3732008Z run 2 meta.inf after update: 2026-08-15T20:22:22.4880827Z run 3 API after second restart: 2026-08-15T20:22:22.4880827Z BUG REPRODUCED: CreateOrUpdateKeyValue changed Created after a restart ``` A server regression test against the current `main` branch also fails: ```text === RUN TestJetStreamFileStreamCreatedTimePreservedAfterRestartAndUpdate jetstream_test.go:6818: Expected created time 2026-08-16 13:22:48.0484564 +0000 UTC after restart and update, got 2026-08-16 13:22:48.0681286 +0000 UTC --- FAIL: TestJetStreamFileStreamCreatedTimePreservedAfterRestartAndUpdate ``` ### Root cause analysis During standalone stream recovery, the stream and filestore are initially constructed using the current server startup time. After recovery, the persisted timestamp is restored only on the stream object: ```go if !cfg.Created.IsZero() { mset.setCreatedTime(cfg.Created) } ``` However, `setCreatedTime` currently updates only `stream.created`. The internal `fileStore.cfg.Created` retains the recovery/startup time. A later `fileStore.UpdateConfig` preserves that stale internal value when writing the new `FileStreamInfo`: ```go newCfg := FileStreamInfo{ Created: fs.cfg.Created, StreamConfig: *cfg, } ``` As a result, the configuration update writes the recovery time to `meta.inf`. The next restart loads and exposes that changed value through the JetStream API. I am preparing a regression test and a small fix that keeps the recovered stream and filestore creation timestamps synchronized.

signals.title: CRITICAL JetStream atomic batch publish leaves per-batch staging directories under <stream>/batches after commit
signals.text: ### Observed behavior Streams created with `AllowAtomicPublish: true` accumulate one directory per batch under ` <store_dir>/jetstream/<account>/streams/<stream>/batches/<batchID>/ ` and these directories are never removed after the batch commits. The count grows monotonically for as long as the server is publishing. Measured on 2.14.5 across 10 file-backed streams, sampling every ~2 minutes: 19:53:45 batch_dirs=6374 logical=13.6GB 19:55:47 batch_dirs=11419 logical=18.6GB 19:57:52 batch_dirs=17301 logical=23.1GB 19:59:59 batch_dirs=23520 logical=27.6GB 20:02:08 batch_dirs=30143 logical=32.2GB 20:04:10 batch_dirs=37394 logical=36.4GB 20:06:11 batch_dirs=43813 logical=40.7GB 20:08:32 batch_dirs=50148 logical=45.9GB 20:10:55 batch_dirs=57614 logical=51.3GB 20:13:20 batch_dirs=65356 logical=56.9GB 20:15:48 batch_dirs=72991 logical=62.3GB 20:18:01 batch_dirs=80047 logical=67.4GB ``` $ ls -la .../streams/stream_name/batches/FU47okxc drwx------. 1 root root 30 Aug 16 19:48 . drwx------. 1 root root 2216896 Aug 16 20:28 .. -rw-------. 1 root root 16 Aug 16 19:48 meta.sum drwx------. 1 root root 10 Aug 16 19:48 msgs drwx------. 1 root root 0 Aug 16 19:48 obs ``` That directory was created when the stream was created and was still present 40 minutes later. Note also the parent directory entry, which had grown to **2,216,896 bytes** for a single stream. **On 2.12.14 the same directories retained the staged message data**, which was considerably worse: the filesystem grew ~2.7 GB/min while total stream bytes stayed flat, eventually filling the node's disk. Upgrading to 2.14.5 stopped the data from being retained but did not stop the directories themselves from accumulating. ### Expected behavior The staging directory for a batch should be removed once the batch is committed (and on abort/expiry). The number of entries under `<stream>/batches/` should stay bounded by the number of in-flight batches, rather than growing without limit for the lifetime of the stream. ### Server and client version Server: `nats:2.14.5-alpine` Also reproduced, in the more severe form where staged message data is retained, on `nats:2.12.14-alpine`. Client: `nats.go` (Go), publishing via the `jetstream` package with atomic batch publish. ### Host environment - Linux x86_64, Kubernetes (k3s), containerd runtime - Server runs as a StatefulSet; JetStream file store on a local NVMe host path - Filesystem: btrfs (metadata profile DUP) - 10 file-backed streams, all `AllowAtomicPublish: true`, aggregate publish rate ~40-50k msgs/sec ### Steps to reproduce Steps to reproduce 1. Create a file-backed stream with atomic batch publish enabled. Ours, via `nats.go`: ```go jetstream.StreamConfig{ Name: "name", Subjects: []string{"name.*"}, Retention: jetstream.LimitsPolicy, Storage: jetstream.FileStorage, Compression: jetstream.S2Compression, MaxAge: time.Hour, MaxBytes: 20 << 30, Duplicates: time.Minute, AllowAtomicPublish: true, } ``` 2. Publish continuously using atomic batches. 3. Watch the directory count under the stream's store: `watch -n 30 'ls -U <store>/jetstream/*/streams/*/batches | wc -l' `

signals.title: [FIXED] Preserve stream created time after recovery
signals.text: During standalone file stream recovery, the persisted creation time was restored on the stream object, but the internal file store configuration retained the server startup time. A subsequent stream configuration update persisted that stale value to `meta.inf`. After another restart, the changed creation time was exposed through the JetStream API. This change keeps the stream and file store creation timestamps synchronized when restoring the persisted creation time. A regression test covers: 1. Creating a file-backed stream. 2. Restarting the server. 3. Updating the stream configuration. 4. Restarting the server again. 5. Verifying that `StreamInfo.Created` remains unchanged. Resolves #8470

Atomic batches would reproduce the existing staged-batch restrictions and preflight all marked conditions under the stream lock before storing any batch member, preserving all-or-nothing behavior. For rolling-upgrade safety, the suggested rollout is: - all supporting binaries always understand and honor the replicated marker, regardless of their local proposal-side flag - proposal-side emission is initially behind a default-off feature flag - every possible stream peer must first run a supporting binary, then the flag must be enabled on every server that can lead the stream - effective support and enablement are verified per server through the existing startup log and `Varz.feature_flags` surface (absent = unsupported, `false` = supported but disabled, `true` = enabled) - unmarked historical entries retain their current behavior This proposal is intentionally limited to `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence`. It does not propose changing message headers, the public error model, sources/mirrors, other consistency headers, or adding a new client capability API. Before implementation I would appreciate confirmation that: 1. the replicated-marker/default-off rollout and existing operational verification surface are acceptable 2. applied per-subject store state is the intended deterministic basis for this check across supported retention modes 3. an apply-time mismatch should consume clustered failed-sequence accounting in the same way as another rejected committed stream entry 4. a marked entry with a missing or invalid predicate should fail closed as a malformed replicated command ### Use case `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` is used as subject-level optimistic concurrency control. A caller reads subject state at sequence S and publishes an update conditional on S still being current. For clustered streams, correctness currently depends on the leader's pre-proposal state and surrounding leadership/readiness mechanisms. The captured-term proposal fence prevents an old-term proposal, but it does not make the conditional predicate part of the replicated state-machine command. Current main has refused every transition route measured, and this proposal does not claim a reproduced production data-loss incident. The objective is to make the existing optimistic-concurrency condition authoritative at the state-machine boundary, so a committed entry whose predicate is stale cannot become valid merely because it crossed a leader transition or was replayed under different in-memory admission state. A deterministic regression can commit a current-term stale conditional entry after a newer value, proving that apply rejects it without relying on leader timing. Removing only the apply-time check then makes the stale value survive, which directly discriminates the proposed mechanism. ### Contribution Yes. I intend to contribute the implementation, including: - backward-compatible replicated encoding - default-off rollout flag and operational verification - normal, fast-batch, and atomic-batch handling - file- and memory-store tests - transform, explicit-subject, compression, restart, replay, catch-up, and sequence-accounting tests - source/mirror and feature-off compatibility tests - a deterministic apply-boundary regression and discriminating mutations
